stem: Fig. 1.1 shows two lamps connected in series with two ammeters. Ammeter A1 reads 0.4 A. (Fig. 1.1)
options: A2 reads 0.2 A, because the current is shared between the two lamps.
A2 reads 0.4 A, because there is only one path for the current.
A2 reads 0.8 A, because current builds up as it goes round.
A2 reads 0 A, because the current is used up by the lamps.
working: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current flows through every component. Current is not used up or shared.
Watch out: 'Used up' is the single most common wrong idea in this topic. Energy is transferred; current is not.

distractors.1: Sharing of current happens at a junction in a PARALLEL circuit. There is no junction here.
distractors.3: Current does not increase round a loop. Charge is conserved.
distractors.4: Lamps convert electrical energy, they do not consume charge.

stem: Fig. 1.2 shows lamps P and Q on separate branches. Both lamps are identical and both are lit. Switch S2 is then opened. (Fig. 1.2)
options: Both P and Q go out.
Q goes out and P stays at the same brightness.
Q goes out and P becomes dimmer.
Q goes out and P becomes brighter.
working: Opening S2 breaks only the lower branch. P is on its own complete branch across the same cell, so the potential difference across P is unchanged and its brightness is unchanged.
Watch out: Read which switch is in which branch before anything else. Trace the loop with your finger.

distractors.1: This is what happens in SERIES. Here each branch is an independent path.
distractors.3: Dimmer would require less pd or more resistance in P's own branch. Neither changed.
distractors.4: A tempting 'more current is now available for P' idea, but the cell's pd across P did not change.

stem: In Fig. 1.3, a student wants to measure the potential difference across the lamp, and also the current through it. (Fig. 1.3)
options: Voltmeter at P, ammeter at R.
Voltmeter at R, ammeter at P.
Voltmeter at Q, ammeter at R.
Voltmeter at R, ammeter at R.
working: A voltmeter goes in parallel ACROSS the component (position R). An ammeter goes in series IN the loop (position P or Q).
Watch out: Memory hook: Ammeter = Along the path. Voltmeter = across the Void beside the component.

distractors.1: Reversed. A voltmeter in series would break the circuit path it is meant to measure across.
distractors.3: Q is in the loop, so it is an ammeter position, not a voltmeter position.
distractors.4: Two meters cannot both occupy the parallel branch and still measure current in the loop.

stem: In Fig. 1.4 the resistance of the variable resistor R is increased. (Fig. 1.4)
options: The ammeter reading increases and lamp L gets brighter.
The ammeter reading decreases and lamp L gets dimmer.
The ammeter reading decreases and lamp L stays the same.
The ammeter reading stays the same and lamp L gets dimmer.
working: Higher resistance opposes the current more, so the current in the single loop falls. Less current through the lamp means it is dimmer.
Watch out: Say the chain out loud: resistance up → current down → lamp dimmer.

distractors.1: Inverts the relationship. More resistance always means less current for the same supply.
distractors.3: The lamp is in the same series loop, so a smaller current must also pass through it.
distractors.4: Brightness cannot change without the current through the lamp changing.

stem: Which row correctly matches an effect of an electric current to an application of that effect?
options: Chemical effect — electric kettle
Heating effect — electroplating a key with copper
Magnetic effect — a crane lifting scrap iron with an electromagnet
Magnetic effect — a fuse melting during a fault
working: A current in a coil produces a magnetic field, which is how an electromagnet works.
Watch out: Three effects, three homes: Chemical = liquids (electrolysis, electroplating). Heating = kettle, toaster, fuse. Magnetic = electromagnet, motor, fan.

distractors.1: A kettle uses the heating effect.
distractors.2: Electroplating is the chemical effect of a current in a liquid.
distractors.4: A fuse melts because of the heating effect.

stem: An appliance normally draws a current of 4.2 A. Which fuse should be fitted?
options: 1 A, so that the circuit breaks as early as possible.
3 A, so that the appliance is protected at all times.
5 A, slightly above the normal working current.
13 A, so that the fuse never needs replacing.
working: The rating must be slightly HIGHER than the normal working current: high enough that the appliance runs, low enough that a fault current melts it.
Watch out: 'Slightly higher' is the mark-scheme phrase. Not 'much higher', not 'equal to'.

distractors.1: A 1 A fuse melts immediately during normal use and the appliance will not switch on.
distractors.2: 3 A is below the 4.2 A working current, so it blows in normal use.
distractors.4: 13 A is far too high. A dangerous fault current would flow without melting the fuse.

stem: Two identical 10 Ω resistors are connected first in series, then in parallel, across the same supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The effective resistance is 20 Ω in series and 5 Ω in parallel, so more current flows in the parallel arrangement.
The effective resistance is 20 Ω in series and 20 Ω in parallel.
The effective resistance is 5 Ω in series and 20 Ω in parallel.
The effective resistance is 10 Ω in both arrangements, because the resistors are identical.
working: Series adds: 10 + 10 = 20 Ω. Parallel provides extra paths, so the effective resistance falls below the smallest resistor; for two equal resistors it halves to 5 Ω. Lower resistance means a larger current.
Watch out: Parallel = more lanes on the expressway = easier flow = lower resistance = bigger current.

distractors.2: Parallel cannot leave the resistance unchanged, because a second path has been added.
distractors.3: Reversed. Adding components in series always increases the effective resistance.
distractors.4: Identical values do not mean identical arrangements behave the same.

stem: Which statement about the kilowatt-hour is correct?
options: It is a unit of power, equal to 1000 watts.
It is a unit of energy, equal to the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour.
It is a unit of current drawn by an appliance in one hour.
It is the cost of running a 1 kW appliance for 1 hour.
working: kWh = power (in kW) × time (in h), so it measures ENERGY. One unit of electricity is 1 kWh.
Watch out: Watt is a rate (energy per second). Watt-hour is a total. Rate × time = total.

distractors.1: 1000 W = 1 kW is the power. The 'hour' part makes it energy.
distractors.3: Current is measured in amperes, not kWh.
distractors.4: Cost = energy in kWh × price per kWh. The kWh itself is not money.

stem:
Fig. 2.1 shows two resistors connected in series to a 12 V supply. (Fig. 2.1)

(a) State what the voltmeter in Fig. 2.1 is measuring.
working: Common error: Writing 'the voltage of the circuit'. The voltmeter reads across one named component only.

stem:
Fig. 2.1 shows two resistors connected in series to a 12 V supply. (Fig. 2.1)

(b) Calculate the effective resistance of the circuit.
answer: Resistors in series, so effective resistance = R1 + R2 = 20 + 40 = 60 Ω (unit required)
working: Common error: Dropping the unit, or halving the values as if they were in parallel.

stem:
Fig. 2.1 shows two resistors connected in series to a 12 V supply. (Fig. 2.1)

(c) R2 is now replaced by an 80 Ω resistor. State and explain what happens to the reading on the ammeter.
answer: The ammeter reading decreases. The effective resistance of the circuit increases (from 60 Ω to 100 Ω). A larger resistance opposes the current more, so a smaller current flows for the same supply.
working: Common error: Stating the answer with no reason. 'State and explain' needs the direction AND the because.

stem:
Fig. 2.1 shows two resistors connected in series to a 12 V supply. (Fig. 2.1)

(d) The two resistors are rearranged in parallel across the same 12 V supply. Explain why the ammeter in the main circuit now reads a larger current.
answer: In parallel there is more than one path for the current, so the effective resistance is lower than either resistor on its own. A lower effective resistance allows a larger current to flow from the supply.
working: Common error: Saying 'parallel is stronger'. The marker wants paths → resistance → current.

stem:
Fig. 2.2 shows the power ratings of five appliances in a flat. Electricity costs $0.32 per kWh. (Fig. 2.2)

(a) The air-conditioner is used for 6 hours every night. Calculate the cost of running it for 30 nights.
answer: Power = 1200 W = 1.2 kW (conversion shown) Energy = 1.2 kW × 6 h × 30 = 216 kWh Cost = 216 × $0.32 = $69.12
working: Common error: Forgetting to divide watts by 1000. Working in W gives an answer 1000× too big.

stem:
Fig. 2.2 shows the power ratings of five appliances in a flat. Electricity costs $0.32 per kWh. (Fig. 2.2)

(b) The kettle has the highest power rating but costs far less per month than the air-conditioner. Explain why.
answer: Energy used depends on power AND the time it is switched on. The kettle is only used for a few minutes at a time, so the total energy in kWh is much smaller despite the higher power rating.
working: Common error: Answering only 'because it uses less electricity', which restates the question.

stem:
Fig. 2.2 shows the power ratings of five appliances in a flat. Electricity costs $0.32 per kWh. (Fig. 2.2)

(c) Suggest two ways the family could reduce their electricity bill, and for each one state the reason it works.
answer: Use the fan instead of the air-conditioner — the fan has a much lower power rating (45 W vs 1200 W), so less energy is used per hour. Switch off appliances when not in use — reduces the number of hours, and energy = power × time. Accept: replace with appliances carrying more energy-efficiency ticks; use the air-con on a timer.
working: Common error: Giving two actions but no reasons. Half the marks here are for the reasons.

stem:
Fig. 2.3 shows part of a room in a flat. (Fig. 2.3)

(a) Identify two electrical hazards shown in Fig. 2.3 and explain the danger of each.
answer: Overloading — too many appliances on one socket means a very large current flows through the wires; the heating effect of this current can overheat the wires and start a fire. Damaged insulation — the bare wire is exposed, so touching it can give a severe electric shock, and sparks can ignite nearby flammable materials.
working: Common error: Naming the hazard without the mechanism. Each hazard is worth 1 mark for the name and 1 for the danger.

stem:
Fig. 2.3 shows part of a room in a flat. (Fig. 2.3)

(b) A person touches a faulty appliance with wet hands and receives a worse shock than they would with dry hands. Explain why.
answer: Wet skin has a much lower resistance than dry skin. A lower resistance allows a larger current to flow through the body, so the shock is more severe.
working: Common error: 'Water conducts electricity' alone does not score. The mark scheme wants resistance → current.

stem:
Fig. 2.3 shows part of a room in a flat. (Fig. 2.3)

(c) State one advantage of a circuit breaker over a fuse.
answer: A circuit breaker can simply be reset and reused, whereas a blown fuse must be replaced.
working: Common error: 'It is safer' is too vague to score.
